steps.title: The legacy model leaks
steps.caption: No layer: Orders calls the ERP directly, and legacy names and codes creep into its own model.
steps.body: With nothing in between, the new Orders service calls the legacy ERP directly, so it has to speak the ERP's language. Legacy names, codes and formats (`CUST_NO`, `STAT_CD = A`, zero-padded keys) turn up in its code, its model and its own database. The new model is now shaped by the old one, and any change in the ERP can break the new service.

steps.title: Translate at the boundary
steps.caption: The layer takes the call in Orders' terms, calls the ERP its way and translates the reply.
steps.body: An **anti-corruption layer** is inserted between the two. Orders asks `getCustomer(42)` in its own language: the **adapter** accepts the call, the **facade** makes the legacy call in the ERP's own terms, and the **translator** maps the reply field by field. A clean `Customer` comes back, and no legacy name crosses into the new model.

steps.title: Legacy changes stop here
steps.caption: The ERP changes a status code: one mapping row is updated, and Orders never notices.
steps.body: The ERP changes a code: an active customer is now `STAT_CD = 01` instead of `A`. One mapping row in the translator is updated to match; the Orders service and its model are untouched and keep working. The layer is the only place that knows both models, so it is the only place that has to change.

steps.title: Keep it thin, then retire
steps.caption: The layer adds a hop and one more thing to run. Once a new service owns customer data, retire it.
steps.body: The price is an extra hop on every call and one more component to run, scale and monitor, so keep the layer thin: translation only, no business rules. In a migration it is temporary: once the customer capability moves to a new Customers service that speaks the new model natively, the layer is retired along with the dependency on the ERP. In front of a third-party or partner system you don't control, it stays for good.
